title: Qibing He
text: Hi! My name is Qibing He, and I am from China. I completed my undergraduate degree in Economics at UBC and am now pursuing a Master of Data Science. I became interested in data science because of its practical value and potential to solve real-world problems. Through the MDS program, I hope to strengthen my technical and analytical skills while gaining hands-on experience working with data.

title: My first weeks in MDS
text:
A moment from my first weeks in the MDS program.


My first weeks in the MDS program have been exciting and full of new experiences. During orientation, I participated in a bingo icebreaker activity that encouraged us to introduce ourselves and learn more about one another. It was a fun way to begin conversations and become more comfortable in a new environment.
Through the activity and other orientation events, I met many new friends from a wide range of professional and educational backgrounds. I also had the opportunity to meet MDS alumni and learn about their experiences in the program. Speaking with them helped me gain a clearer understanding of what to expect from the program and how the skills we develop can be applied after graduation. We also shared lunch during orientation, which gave us time to continue our conversations in a relaxed setting.
During the first week of classes, I began to understand how the different courses fit together. In DSCI 511, I started learning the foundations of programming with Python. DSCI 521 introduced Git, GitHub, the terminal, and data science workflows, while DSCI 523 focused on R and data processing. In DSCI 551, I began reviewing the foundations of probability and statistics. Although the first week introduced many new tools and concepts, it made me excited to see how these subjects will connect throughout the MDS program.

title: Distribution of Parks Across Vancouver
text:
This post examines how public parks are distributed across Vancouver’s neighbourhoods. I will use Python to inspect the data, summarize the number of parks in each neighbourhood, and visualize the results.
Data: Parks, City of Vancouver Open Data Portal. The dataset is provided under the Open Government Licence – Vancouver.

title: Distribution of Parks Across Vancouver
text:
Setup
The following chunk loads the Python packages used in this analysis and shows the Python executable used by Quarto.

import sys
import pandas as pd
import altair as alt

Check and clean the data
Before counting parks by neighbourhood, I check the variables used in the analysis for missing values. Records without a neighbourhood or park area are excluded from the cleaned dataset.

analysis_columns = ["Name", "NeighbourhoodName", "Hectare"]

missing_summary = (
    parks[analysis_columns]
    .isna()

    .to_frame()
)

title: Distribution of Parks Across Vancouver
text:
Parks by neighbourhood
I group the cleaned data by neighbourhood and count the number of parks in each area. The table below shows the ten neighbourhoods with the most parks.

park_counts = (
    parks_clean
    .groupby("NeighbourhoodName")
    .size()
    .reset_index(name="park_count")
    .sort_values("park_count", ascending=False)

title: Distribution of Parks Across Vancouver
text:
Visualize the distribution
The following bar chart compares the number of public parks across Vancouver’s neighbourhoods.

park_chart = (
    alt.Chart(park_counts)
    .mark_bar(color="#2a9d8f")
    .encode(
        x=alt.X(
            "park_count:Q",
            title="Number of parks"
        ),
        y=alt.Y(
            "NeighbourhoodName:N",
            sort="-x",
            title="Neighbourhood"
        ),
        tooltip=[
            alt.Tooltip(
                "NeighbourhoodName:N",
                title="Neighbourhood"
            ),
            alt.Tooltip(
                "park_count:Q",
                title="Number of parks"
            )
        ]
    )
    .properties(
        width=650,
        height=500
    )
)

park_chart









Figure 1: Number of public parks in each Vancouver neighbourhood.

title: Distribution of Parks Across Vancouver
text:
Findings
The dataset contains 218 parks across 22 Vancouver neighbourhoods, and there are no missing values in the three variables used for this analysis. Downtown has the largest number of parks, with 23. Kitsilano and Hastings-Sunrise follow with 16 parks each. The results show that the number of parks is not evenly distributed across neighbourhoods, although this analysis counts parks and does not account for differences in park size.

title: Park Sizes in Vancouver
text:
This post examines the distribution of public park sizes in Vancouver. I will use R to inspect park areas, calculate summary statistics, identify the largest parks, and visualize the distribution of park sizes.
Data: Parks, City of Vancouver Open Data Portal. The dataset is provided under the Open Government Licence – Vancouver.

title: Park Sizes in Vancouver
text:
Setup
The following chunk loads the R package used for visualization.

library(ggplot2)

title: Park Sizes in Vancouver
text:
Load and inspect the data
First, I load the parks dataset and inspect its dimensions and selected columns.

parks <- read.csv(
  "../../data/parks.csv",
  sep = ";",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

cat(
  "The dataset contains",
  nrow(parks),
  "parks and",
  ncol(parks),
  "columns.\n"
)

The dataset contains 218 parks and 15 columns.

head(parks[c("Name", "NeighbourhoodName", "Hectare")])

                   Name NeighbourhoodName Hectare
1  Arbutus Village Park     Arbutus-Ridge    1.41
2        Trafalgar Park     Arbutus-Ridge    4.85
3         Coopers' Park          Downtown    1.71
4 Devonian Harbour Park          Downtown    4.42
5     Emery Barnes Park          Downtown    0.85
6      Wendy Poole Park          Downtown    0.04

title: Park Sizes in Vancouver
text:
Check and clean the data
I check the variables used in the analysis for missing values before calculating park-size statistics.

analysis_columns <- c(
  "Name",
  "NeighbourhoodName",
  "Hectare"
)

colSums(is.na(parks[analysis_columns]))

             Name NeighbourhoodName           Hectare 
                0                 0                 0 



parks_clean <- parks[
  complete.cases(parks[analysis_columns]),
]

parks_clean$Hectare <- as.numeric(
  parks_clean$Hectare
)

parks_clean <- parks_clean[
  !is.na(parks_clean$Hectare),
]

cat(
  nrow(parks_clean),
  "parks remain after cleaning.\n"
)

218 parks remain after cleaning.

title: Park Sizes in Vancouver
text:
Summary of park sizes
I calculate several summary statistics to understand the typical park size and the overall range of park areas.

size_summary <- data.frame(
  Statistic = c(
    "Mean",
    "Median",
    "Minimum",
    "Maximum"
  ),
  Hectares = round(
    c(
      mean(parks_clean$Hectare),
      median(parks_clean$Hectare),
      min(parks_clean$Hectare),
      max(parks_clean$Hectare)
    ),
    2
  )
)

size_summary

title: Park Sizes in Vancouver
text:
Largest parks
The following table identifies the ten largest parks in the dataset.

largest_parks <- parks_clean[
  order(
    parks_clean$Hectare,
    decreasing = TRUE
  ),
  c(
    "Name",
    "NeighbourhoodName",
    "Hectare"
  )
]

title: Park Sizes in Vancouver
text:
Visualize the largest parks
The following chart compares the areas of the ten largest parks in the dataset.

top_ten_parks <- head(largest_parks, 10)

ggplot(
  top_ten_parks,
  aes(
    x = reorder(Name, Hectare),
    y = Hectare
  )
) +
  geom_col(fill = "#457b9d") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    x = "Park",
    y = "Area (hectares)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 1: The ten largest public parks in Vancouver by area.

title: Park Sizes in Vancouver
text:
Findings
The 218 parks in the dataset have a mean area of 6.2 hectares but a median area of only 1.4 hectares. This large difference indicates that the distribution of park sizes is strongly right-skewed: most parks are relatively small, while a few very large parks increase the mean. Stanley Park is the largest at 400 hectares, considerably larger than Fraserview Golf Course, the second-largest site at 84.34 hectares.
